newsitem.title: USA: Taiwan news should further lift U.S. hog prices.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan news should further lift U.S. hog prices.

text.p: U.S. hog prices have posted sharp gains since Thursday on optimism pork exports will jump to cover the loss of Taiwanese pork exports, and analysts expect more price gains but probably at a slower pace.

John Lawrence, extension economist at Iowa State University, said after the Taiwan news he raised by $3.00 per hundredweight (cwt) his average U.S. hog price estimate for 1997, basis Iowa interior markets.
"This says we would average maybe $58 for the year," he said, versus his original $55 estimated average.

Dale Benson, analyst with Dean Witter Reynolds, said the greater demand could lift June lean hog futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange to 85.00 to 90.00 cents a lb in June, which would be a live-hog equivalent of $66.00 per cwt. CME June hogs Monday ended at 82.150 cents, up the 2.00-cent limit and hogs sold on a live basis in Iowa at $50 per cwt.
In 1996, Taiwan shipped 266,225 tonnes of pork to Japan versus 141,790 from the U.S, according to Japan's Ministry of Finance figures released by the U.S. Meat Export Federation.
"I think we would pick up half of that business fairly easily. That would virtually double our exports to Japan," said Benson.

Jack Weaver, analyst with Refco Inc, also on Monday said U.S. cash hog prices should rally to the mid-$50 per cwt area by summer and may reach the high $50s or $60 if U.S. exports grow enough because of Taiwan's pork export ban. However, he expected the rise to be short-lived with a drop to the $40s expected by fall amid expanding hog production.
Some analysts cautioned that food-safety concerns in Japan plus a strong dollar versus the yen could restrict the amount of U.S. pork Japan buys.
"We are getting very excited before they (the sales) actually happen," said Paul Georgy, president of Allendale Inc, an agricultural research firm.

Cash pork prices also sped higher in the wake of the Taiwan news, but John Kleist, director of research for ING Futures and Options, attributed the gains to U.S. supermarkets rushing to buy pork before the Japanese buying starts.
The U.S. Agriculture Department reported U.S. pork cutout values on Friday jumped $2.12 to $1.93 per cwt from Thursday when the Taiwan news broke.

Foot-and-mouth disease is not harmful to humans, but is highly contagious to hogs, cattle and sheep. It causes blistering around the animal's mouth, feet and udders, making it difficult to eat, especially for young animals.

Analysts noted that this outbreak comes after an E.coli outbreak in Japan and amid global concerns about Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease in beef -- all of which could curtail meat consumption in Japan.

"Pork, regardless where it comes from, could get a bad rap in Japan," said Doug Harper, senior livestock analyst with Brock and Associates. "It is very possible if they cut back on pork consumption, there may not be a void to fill or as large a void to fill."

There is a heightened concern about the safety of imported meat in Japan, but Japanese health officials as well as U.S. meat industry representatives have been working to assure the Japanese that foot-and-mouth disease is not a threat to humans.
"This is something our people in Tokyo were quick to stress. This doesn't present a threat in any way to peoples' health," said Jeff Oates, spokesman for the Denver-based U.S. Meat Export Federation.
